items.title: Capture Guide
items.text:
Capture Guide is an iPhone app for recording a scene, such as a room or an outdoor area, for 3D Gaussian Splatting (a way of turning photos into a 3D model you can view from any angle). While you walk, the phone trains a rough reconstruction from the frames it has taken so far and marks the places that are still weak. You see those marks in AR and walk there before you leave the scene.

Every capture is also saved as a posed dataset (the photos plus where the camera was for each one), ready for the training software of your choice.

flowchart LR
    A[Walk and capture] --> B[The phone trains a reconstruction]
    B --> C[Guidance shows weak spots]
    C -->|Walk there| A
    A -->|Scene covered| D[Stop and export]

Clip pending: guidance in AR

  • Capturing a scene: how to walk through a scene and which frames the app skips.
  • Reading the guidance: what the coloured dots and the yellow camera tell you.
  • Your captures and exporting: looking through captures on the phone, getting them off it and training them.
  • Troubleshooting and FAQ: what to do when tracking is lost or the phone runs hot, and what the error messages mean.

items.title: Capturing a scene
items.text: How to record a scene with Capture Guide. The app is built for scenes: rooms and other spaces, indoors or outdoors. It has no mode for small objects.

items.title: Overlap and viewpoint variety
items.text:
A 3D reconstruction needs every part of the scene in several photos taken from different places. Two rules follow from that.

Move between shots. The app takes a keyframe (a photo it keeps for the reconstruction) when the view has changed enough against the last one. By default that means the new view shares about 60% or less with the last keyframe ("Photo overlap" in Settings, which opens with the gear at the bottom right of the camera screen), or you have turned the phone by about 10 degrees. Standing still adds nothing. A turn on the spot does add a frame every so often, which keeps the keyframes linked, but a step sideways gives the reconstruction the new angle it needs.

Do not retrace yourself. If you stand close to an earlier keyframe and look the same way, within about 10 degrees, the app skips the frame. "Close" scales with how far away the surfaces are: from 5 cm up to 30 cm. Come back to a spot from a different direction and it counts again.

items.title: Walking pace and distance
items.text:
Walk slowly and keep the phone steady. The app measures how much the image smears: the faster you turn the phone, the more blur, and a dim room makes it worse because the camera exposes longer. A frame that smears by more than about 2 pixels is skipped, and the frame count in the pill at the top stops rising. Slow down, and it picks up again.

The app does not enforce a distance to the surfaces. Check the guidance and the keyframe flashes to see whether the phone is picking up your view.

items.title: Angles
items.text:
Look at the same wall or piece of furniture from more than one side. A sideways step changes the view of nearby surfaces far more than a turn does, and that change in angle is one of the triggers for a new keyframe. For the floor and ceiling, tilt the phone down or up while you walk.

The guidance helps with this: it shows a yellow camera where to stand and the outlined area you should point at. Reading the guidance explains it.

items.title: Light
items.text: Bright, even light gives sharp frames. In a dim room the camera exposes longer, so the same movement smears more and more frames are skipped for blur. Turn on the lights or move more slowly. In general, steady lighting through the whole capture gives a more even result than light that changes as you go.

items.title: Reflective surfaces
items.text: In general, mirrors and glass reconstruct poorly, and so do other very shiny surfaces, because what they show changes with your viewpoint. Expect weak results there.

items.title: Motion in the scene
items.text: A reconstruction assumes the scene stands still. In general, anything that moves while you capture, such as people or traffic, can show up as smears in the result. Wait for it to pass when you can.

items.title: Keyframes by hand
items.text:
If you want full control, turn on manual capture with the hand button on the side rail. The automatic keyframes stop, and while you record, a round shutter button appears above the rail. Tapping it takes a keyframe from the next sharp frame. If none arrives within about half a second, the button flashes red; hold the phone still and try again.

Screenshot pending: a white border around the screen at the moment of a keyframe.

items.title: When tracking is lost
items.text:
The app only captures while the phone's tracking (Apple's ARKit) is working normally. If tracking drops, for example from fast motion or a scene with too little detail, capture pauses and the phone tries to find its place again.

  • While it searches, a banner with an orange arrows symbol reads "Relocalising — move back to where you were. Starting a new segment in N s." Walk back to where you were. If the phone recognises the place, capture continues in the same segment.
  • If it has not found the place after 15 seconds, or you tap "Start new segment here", capture continues in a new segment. While tracking restarts, the banner reads "Tracking restarting — a new segment starts when tracking returns.", and a second banner with a yellow tortoise reads "Move the phone slowly around to start tracking."

A segment is one continuous capture in one coordinate system. The phone starts a new one when it has lost the old coordinate system. Each segment is saved in its own folder, and the guidance starts over: the old reconstruction is no longer shown, and the ring around Stop comes back once the new segment has its first coverage figure. A capture with more than one segment shows "2 seg" (or more) on its card in your captures, and its Frames tab lists the segments one by one. You can tap "Start new segment here" during the countdown when you do not want to go back.

Screenshot pending: the dark relocalising banner under the status pill, with its orange symbol, the countdown and the "Start new segment here" button.

items.title: An indoor room
items.text:
Walk the room and follow the guidance. The app shows a yellow camera where to stand next and an outlined area to point at. When it reports "Room covered", it has no further target.

With LiDAR, grey diagonal hatching appears on surfaces the phone sees that the reconstruction does not cover yet. It disappears once you have captured them. Without LiDAR, or with Live splat set to "Off", there is no hatching, so rely on the coloured quality dots (they show how well each part of the scene is covered) and the map.

items.title: An outdoor walk
items.text:
Before you tap Record, set "Scene" to "Outdoor" in Settings. The engine then trains with a sky background and uses larger cells. The setting can't be changed during a capture.

Beyond the range of LiDAR, and on phones without it, the phone estimates depth from the image alone, so distant surfaces still get guidance.

Moving people and traffic add the problem described above.

items.title: Keeping the screen on
items.text: While a capture runs, the phone does not dim or lock the screen. After you tap Stop, the usual screen timeout applies again as soon as the phone has finished saving the capture.

items.title: Your captures and exporting
items.text: How to find your captures on the iPhone, look through them, share them, and train one into a 3D Gaussian Splatting model on your computer with the free Spirula Studio app.

items.title: Your captures
items.text:
Tap the picture at the bottom left of the camera screen to see your captures, newest first. Each card shows four photos from the capture with its name, date and place, the number of frames and its size. "Close" at the top left takes you back to the camera.

  • Names: a capture is named after its place and time, for example "Main Street, Lucerne · 16:45", or after its date and time when there is no place. To rename it, open it and tap its name at the top.
  • Deleting: tap "Select", tap the captures you want to remove (a check mark appears at the bottom right of each), then tap "Delete" at the bottom and confirm. This cannot be undone.
  • At the larger accessibility text sizes the cards are shown one per row.

Your captures, newest first.

items.title: Looking at a capture
items.text:
Tap a card to open it. The back button at the top left takes you back to your captures; it shows a chevron, with the word "Captures" on iOS 18. The share button at the top right is described below. The capture has three tabs.

Overview: the capture seen from above. Grey points are the surfaces, and a coloured line from a dot to an arrowhead is the path you walked, one colour per segment. Pinch to zoom, drag to move, double-tap to reset. A capture without saved camera positions shows "No top view" instead. Below it, the facts follow one per row: date and time, place, number of frames, number of segments and size. A small square map with a pin sits next to them and shows where you were; at the larger accessibility text sizes it sits above them, and a capture without a recorded place has no map. A strip of photos follows. "Done" at the bottom takes you back to the camera.

Frames: every keyframe, segment by segment. Tap one to see it large; "Exclude" leaves it out of the export, "Restore" brings it back. To change several at once, tap "Select" above the grid, tap the frames, then "Exclude" or "Restore" at the bottom. Excluded frames are greyed out and marked with a crossed-out eye. Nothing is deleted: the photo stays on the phone, and only the list of photos that exports read (transforms.json) leaves it out. If the 3D model was built before you excluded frames, a note says that it still contains them.

Splat: the 3D model the phone built, if there is one. Drag to orbit, pinch to zoom. When more than one segment has a model, a picker above it chooses the segment. Without a model, the tab says why: "Live splat was off", "Built on the Mac" or "No splat yet".

The Overview tab.

The Frames tab; the first two frames are excluded.

The Splat tab.

items.title: Where your captures are stored
items.text:
Every capture is saved on the phone while you record, with nothing to switch on. Open the Files app and go to On My iPhone, then "Capture Guide". Each capture is a folder named after its start time in UTC, for example 2026-10-07T12-30-00Z. Inside it you find:

  • capture.json: the capture's name, place and which frames you excluded.
  • thumb-v2.jpg: the picture on the capture's card. Captures from older versions of the app also have a thumb.jpg, which you can ignore.
  • overlay-metrics.jsonl: a working file you can ignore.
  • One folder per segment: segment-0, segment-1 and so on. A segment is one continuous stretch of capture in one coordinate system (Capturing a scene explains when a new one starts).

A segment folder holds:

  • images/: the full-resolution photo of every keyframe. The photos are stored as the camera sensor records them, turned sideways; the app shows them upright, and training software uses them as they are.
  • transforms.json: where the camera was for each photo, and its lens settings. Frames you excluded are left out of it. Once you exclude a frame, transforms.unfiltered.json keeps the full list.
  • depth/: the LiDAR depth maps. The folder exists in every segment and stays empty without LiDAR.
  • points.ply: a sparse cloud of coloured points the phone tracked.
  • splat.ply: the 3D model (made of many splats) the phone trained while you captured, written after you tap Stop or when a new segment starts. It is there only for captures with Live splat on "This iPhone".
  • overlap_audit.json and wire/: working files of the app that you can ignore.

Tap Stop before you leave the app. While you capture, the photos are written straight away, but the list in transforms.json is updated after every tenth keyframe and when a segment ends. Stopping updates it too. If the app closes in between, the newest photos stay in images/ but are missing from the list. Sometimes a new segment starts just before Stop. It leaves an empty segment-N folder behind that you can skip.

Screenshot pending: the Files app at On My iPhone, "Capture Guide", with one dated capture folder open and its segment-0 folder showing its files.

items.title: Getting captures off the phone
items.text:
The quickest way is the share button at the top right of an open capture. It packs the capture into one zip file, without the app's working copies in wire/, and opens the iOS share sheet: send it with AirDrop to your Mac, save it to Files, or mail it. Unzipped, it gives the capture folder with its segment folders, ready for Capture to COLMAP below. The button waits until the capture is saved on the iPhone.

Screenshot pending: the iOS share sheet after tapping the share button, with the capture's zip file and AirDrop.

The folder is also shared with the Files app, so the usual iOS ways work. Press and hold a capture folder in Files to copy it to iCloud Drive or another location. With the phone connected to a Mac by cable, the Capture Guide folder also shows in Finder under the phone's file sharing. A capture can be large, because it holds full-resolution photos.

Copy the whole capture folder, or at least the segment folders you want. A segment folder has to stay in one piece, because the photos and transforms.json belong together.

items.title: Choosing a segment
items.text: Each segment has its own coordinate system, so you train each one separately; they cannot be joined into one model. In general, start with the segment that has the most photos.

items.title: Turning a segment into a COLMAP model
items.text:
Many 3DGS trainers, Spirula Studio among them, read a COLMAP model (a folder with the photos and the camera positions in a standard layout). The phone writes its own layout instead, so you convert it with the Capture to COLMAP app. This is the default route. If you want to skip the conversion, see "The quick route" below.

Download CaptureToColmap-macos-arm64.zip from the latest release and unzip it. It runs on a Mac with Apple Silicon and macOS 14 or newer; a Windows version is planned. The app is not signed, so macOS blocks it at first. Double-click the app once and click "Done" on the warning that macOS cannot check it for malicious software. Then open System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down to the message that "Capture to COLMAP was blocked", click "Open Anyway" and confirm. From then on it opens normally.

To use it:

  1. Open Capture to COLMAP.
  2. Next to "Segment folder", click "Choose…" and pick one segment folder, such as segment-0.
  3. "Output folder" is filled in with the same name plus _colmap, next to the segment. Change it with "Choose…" if you like.
  4. Leave "Camera positions" and "Photo matching" on their recommended entries. "Refine with the phone's positions (recommended)" matches the photos to each other, starting from where the phone thought the camera was, and keeps the result at real-world scale. The other entry, "Use the phone's positions as they are", skips that fit. "Neighbouring photos (recommended)" compares each photo with the ones taken around it. "Every photo with every other (slow; short captures only)" compares all of them. "Match checking" can stay on "Standard (recommended)". If many photos are missing from the result, export again with "Relaxed, checked against the phone's tracking (more photos, slower)". It places more photos and checks them more thoroughly against the phone's positions, which takes longer.
  5. Leave "Starting points" on its recommended entry too. It writes seed.ply, a cloud built from the phone's depth sensor and the phone's own points, together with COLMAP's points, coloured from your photos. Spirula Studio can start training from it.
  6. Leave "Depth images" on Phone LiDAR. It writes the depth sensor's readings next to the photos, which some trainers can use as a guide for the geometry.
  7. Click "Export". The app shows the elapsed time and a status line. "Show details" opens the log.
  8. When the status line says "Done", click "Show in Finder" to open the output folder.

The output folder holds:

  • images/: copies of the photos, so the folder works on its own and you can move it.
  • sparse/0/: the COLMAP model.
  • seed.ply: the starting points for training (absent when Starting points is None or nothing could be built).
  • depths/: the phone's depth sensor readings for each photo (absent when Depth images is None or the capture has no depth sensor data).
  • work/: the app's working files, which the trainer does not need.

Photos that the app cannot match well enough are left out of the model. Exporting the same segment again replaces the earlier export.

Screenshot pending: the Capture to COLMAP window with a segment folder chosen, the output folder filled in, all four dropdowns on their recommended entries and the "Export" button visible.

items.title: Training
items.text:
Spirula Studio is a free, open-source app that trains a 3D Gaussian Splatting model from your photos. It has a desktop app for Macs with Apple Silicon, Windows and Linux. Download it from its releases page. The downloaded Mac build is signed without an Apple developer certificate, so macOS may block the first open. If it does, the same "Open Anyway" step in Privacy & Security applies as for Capture to COLMAP above.

There are two routes. Both work.

items.title: Default: through Capture to COLMAP
items.text:
1. Convert the segment with Capture to COLMAP, as described above. The conversion refines the camera positions the phone recorded.
  2. Open the output folder, the one with images/ and sparse/0/, in Spirula Studio.
  3. Choose seed.ply from the output folder as the seed point cloud ("Seed point cloud PLY"). This needs Spirula Studio 2026.10.6 or newer; with an older version, skip this step. A long capture can give a seed.ply with more than a million points. You don't need to do anything about it: Spirula Studio's source code shows that it then starts from a random subset as large as its splat limit (one million by default), and in a test on one capture a cloud thinned to 300,000 points trained nearly as well as the full one.
  4. To let Spirula Studio use the depth images, set its depth supervision weight above 0 (command line: --depth-supervision-weight 0.1); at its default of 0 they are ignored. In our tests they placed surfaces at the measured distance and removed see-through spots in an indoor capture; in an outdoor capture they did not change how the trained scene looked from new viewpoints.
  5. Start training and watch the preview until it looks good, then save the result as a .ply file and open it in a splat viewer.

items.title: The quick route: straight from the phone's folder
items.text:
1. Open a segment folder, such as segment-0, directly in Spirula Studio. It reads the segment's transforms.json and points.ply, so there is no conversion step.
  2. Start training and save the result as in the default route.

This route trains on the camera positions as the phone recorded them and skips the refinement that Capture to COLMAP does.

For the exact buttons, see the Spirula Studio project page. Other 3DGS trainers that read COLMAP also work from the same output folder. In general, a computer can use more splats and larger images than the phone's engine does, so the result tends to be cleaner than the splat.ply from the phone.

You can also open the phone's splat.ply directly in a splat viewer that reads .ply files, which is a quick check of what the phone built.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: What you need, how the camera screen is laid out, and your first capture.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• An iPhone with iOS 18 or newer. Capture Guide was tested on an iPhone 14 Pro.
  • A LiDAR sensor is optional. With LiDAR, the app saves a depth map (a distance for each pixel) with each photo it keeps and draws grey hatching over surfaces the reconstruction does not cover yet. Without LiDAR the capture still works, without those two. On a phone without the sensor, "Use LiDAR" in Settings is greyed out.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Coming soon

Capture Guide will be available through TestFlight or the App Store. The links will appear here.

Capture Guide opens straight into the camera, so iOS asks for camera access the first time the camera starts. iOS also asks whether the app may use the local network. The app uses it only to look for a Mac running the planned companion app; building the 3D model on this iPhone does not need it.

The first time you tap Record, iOS asks for your location. The app saves where a capture was made, so it can name the capture after the place and show it on a map. Recording starts right away, whatever you answer.

items.title: The camera screen
items.text:
Screenshot pending: the camera screen before recording, with the side rail on the right, the "Splat: iPhone" chip above the Record button, the newest capture at the bottom left and the gear at the bottom right.

  • Record, at the bottom in the middle, starts a capture. Nothing is saved before you tap it.
  • The Live splat chip above Record shows where the 3D model is built while you capture, for example "Splat: iPhone". The model is made of many splats, tiny blobs of colour. Tap the chip to change where it is built.
  • Your captures: the picture at the bottom left shows your newest capture. Tap it to see all of them. It appears after your first capture.
  • Settings: the gear at the bottom right.
  • The side rail on the right edge has one button per guidance layer. A white disc behind a button means that layer is on. Reading the guidance lists the buttons.

The controls on the camera screen stay dark, also when your iPhone is set to Light Mode, as in the Camera app.

items.title: Your first capture
items.text:
The phone builds the 3D model itself, so you need no other device.

  1. Open Capture Guide. While the screen reads "Preparing splat engine…", the app tunes its engine for your phone. The camera appears when it is ready.
  2. Leave the chip on "Splat: iPhone".
  3. Tap Record. A pill at the top shows the tracking state and a count, for example "Tracking · 0 frames". The number counts keyframes, the photos the app keeps.
  4. Walk slowly and keep the camera on the scene. Each time the app takes a keyframe, a white border flashes once around the screen. Capturing a scene explains how to walk.
  5. Follow the guidance. A white ring around the Stop button fills as more of the scene is covered; it appears once the phone has a first coverage figure. Reading the guidance explains each part.
  6. When "Room covered" appears, or when you have everything you want, tap Stop.
  7. The capture opens. While the phone still writes the 3D model, the button at the bottom reads "Saving splat…". Then it reads "Done", and the line above it says what was saved, for example "Saved with splat".
  8. Tap Done to go back to the camera. The capture stays on the phone: open it from the picture at the bottom left, or find it in the Files app. Your captures and exporting shows what you can do with it.

Screenshot pending: the camera screen while recording, with the status pill and the guidance line at the top, the quality dots on the scene, the round map at the bottom left and the ring around the Stop button.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Tap the gear, or the Live splat chip. Settings that change how the camera runs can't be changed during a capture; they read "Stop to change." until you tap Stop.

  • Live splat: where the 3D model is built while you capture.
    • "This iPhone" is the default. If the phone cannot start its engine, the chip adds "(unavailable)".
    • "Mac" is for the planned Mac companion app. Macs found on your network appear in a list, and you can type an address. If no Mac answers within a few seconds, the capture runs without a 3D model and the chip adds "(not found)".
    • "Off" builds no 3D model and keeps the phone cooler. The guidance still works, without the grey hatching.
  • Use LiDAR: on by default on phones with the sensor.
  • Scene: "Indoor" or "Outdoor". Outdoor trains the model with a sky background and uses larger cells, for scenes that reach far away.
  • Photo overlap: how much of its view a new keyframe may share with the one before. "Splatting 60 %" is the default. "SfM-safe 72 %" takes more photos, which suits photogrammetry software.
  • Guidance sounds and Proximity ticks: see Guidance sounds and taps.
  • Coverage colours: the colours of the quality dots and the map. "Blue-Orange" is the default; "Cividis" runs from dark blue to yellow.

Settings; some rows explain themselves in a grey second line.

Info

A Mac companion app is planned. Capture Guide does not need it.

items.title: Reading the guidance
items.text:
What the on-screen guidance tells you while you capture, and what to do about each part.

Most of it is drawn over the camera image. The phone keeps its own map of the surfaces it has seen and how well your photos cover them, and with Live splat on "This iPhone" it also trains a rough 3D model as you walk. The first dots and hatching show up a little while after you tap Record, once there is something to judge. With Live splat set to "Off", the dots, the map, the progress ring and the next-view targets still work; only the grey hatching and the 3D model are missing.

items.title: The side rail
items.text:
The buttons on the right edge switch the guidance layers on and off. A white disc behind a button means on; a plain white symbol means off. From top to bottom:

  • Splat view (a cube): shows the 3D model instead of the camera image. It appears once the phone has built part of the model, with Live splat on "This iPhone". See Splat view.
  • Quality dots (a grid of dots). See Quality dots.
  • Hatch (stacked layers): the grey hatching. It appears when the phone uses LiDAR (a phone with the sensor and "Use LiDAR" on in Settings) and Live splat is not "Off". See Grey hatching.
  • Next-view targets (binoculars). See Next-view target.
  • Keyframe frustums (a pyramid). See Keyframe frustums.
  • Manual capture (a hand). See Keyframes by hand.

While the splat view is on, only the splat view and manual capture buttons stay.

At the larger accessibility text sizes, touch and hold a button to see it enlarged with its name.

Screenshot pending: the side rail on the right edge, with quality dots, next-view targets and keyframe frustums on (white discs) and the hatch and manual capture off.

items.title: Progress ring
items.text:
What you see. While you record, a white ring around the Stop button fills up. It appears a little after you start, once the phone has its first coverage figure.

What it means. The filled part is the share of the known surface that is nearly fully covered: the surface is split into small patches, and a patch counts once its coverage is above 80% (Quality dots explains coverage). The ring grows as you fill gaps. When a new segment starts, the ring disappears until the new segment has its own figure. With VoiceOver on, the Stop button reads the figure, for example "63 % covered".

What to do. Use it to judge how far along you are. It rarely reaches the full circle: corners you cannot reach and surfaces seen from one side keep it below that. "Room covered" in the guidance line is the better sign that you are done.

Screenshot pending: the Stop button with its white ring about two-thirds filled.

items.title: Quality dots
items.text:
What you see. Small dots floating over the scene, on the surfaces the phone knows. With the default colour scheme, "Blue-Orange", a light blue dot is well covered, the colour turns darker as coverage gets worse, and orange means the spot needs work. The map legend (below) always shows the scheme you picked, from "good" to "needs work".

What it means. A spot gets full marks when the phone has seen it in about 8 photos, taken from a spread of directions, with at least one of them close enough to show it sharply. Fewer photos, or photos from one side only, leave the dot towards orange. The colours change as the phone takes new keyframes.

What to do. Walk towards the orange dots and look at them from a new side. Moving sideways helps more than turning on the spot, for the reasons given in Capturing a scene.

Turn the dots off with the "Quality dots" button on the side rail; the guidance keeps working either way. "Coverage colours" in Settings switches the colour scheme.

Screenshot pending: a room in the camera view with quality dots, light blue on a well-covered wall and orange on a weakly covered corner, with the ring around the Stop button visible.

items.title: Splat view
items.text:
What you see. With the "Splat view" button on, the camera image and the other layers give way to the 3D model itself on black, so you can see what the phone has built so far. The map stays.

What it means. Gaps and thin areas in the splat view are places the model has not learned yet.

What to do. Switch the splat view on for a quick look, then off again to carry on with the guidance. While it is on, next-view targets are paused.

Screenshot pending: the splat view of a partly built room on black, with the "Splat view" button on (white disc) in the side rail.

items.title: Grey hatching
items.text:
What you see. Grey diagonal stripes over a faint grey fill, lying on the surfaces the sensor has found.

What it means. The LiDAR sensor has found a surface here, but the reconstruction has nothing within about 10 cm of it yet. Hatching needs LiDAR and a Live splat setting other than "Off". It also stays off until the first reconstruction exists, so you do not see it in the first moments of a capture.

What to do. Point the camera at the hatched surfaces. The stripes disappear as the reconstruction catches up.

Screenshot pending: grey diagonal hatching on part of a wall and floor, with the already reconstructed part of the same wall free of it.

items.title: Keyframe frustums
items.text:
What you see. A thin outline of a pyramid at every place where the app took a keyframe, pointing the way the camera looked. It is on by default.

What it means. The colour tells you how well that keyframe is tied to the others: it runs from "needs work" at 0% to "good" at 72%, the share of its view that another keyframe also sees. A white pyramid means the app cannot judge that keyframe yet. A new segment clears them, because the old coordinate system is gone.

What to do. Where pyramids sit at the "needs work" end, add views in between and around them, so each keyframe shares more of its view with its neighbours.

Switch them with the "Keyframe frustums" button on the side rail. Like the dots and the hatching, they are hidden in the splat view.

Screenshot pending: pyramid outlines along a walked path, most of them blue and one or two orange where keyframes are far apart.

items.title: Next-view target
items.text:
What you see. A yellow camera shape in the room, with a ring on the floor under it, and an outlined box around the area to capture. When you are close to the yellow camera, a ring appears at the area itself. If the yellow camera is outside the screen, a white arrowhead near the screen edge points towards it.

A line near the top, under the status pill and any banners, tells you what to do next. These are the lines, as they appear:

  • "Stand at the yellow camera and point it at the outlined area": you are still far from it.
  • "Point at the outlined area": you are at the yellow camera but not yet looking the right way.
  • "Turn toward the outlined area": the same, with an arrow showing which way to turn.
  • "Good — hold steady": you are in position, and the whole target turns green.
  • "Captured": the target is done. It stays for a second.
  • "Keep scanning — the next view appears shortly": weak areas remain, but there is no target to show right now.

"Room covered" appears in green in the same place when no weak area is left.

What it means. The app picks one weak area at a time and shows you where to stand to fix it. You are in position when you are within about half a metre of the yellow camera and looking roughly at the area. With automatic keyframes on, the app then takes a keyframe by itself, you feel a tap, and you hear a click. If you use manual capture, tap the shutter button yourself.

A target ends in one of four ways:

  • A keyframe is taken while you are in position. You hear a tone and feel a tap, "Captured" shows, and the next target follows.
  • Other photos you take cover the area first.
  • You do not approach for about 20 seconds. The app drops the target and may offer another.
  • Another area becomes clearly more important.

No target shows during the first 20 seconds of a segment. Targets also need the "Next-view targets" button on (it is on by default) and a running capture, and they pause in the splat view.

What to do. Walk to the yellow camera and point the phone at the outlined area. When "Room covered" shows, you can stop, or carry on if you want a denser capture.

Screenshot pending: a room with the yellow camera shape, the ring on the floor below it, the outlined box on a wall, and the instruction line "Stand at the yellow camera and point it at the outlined area" under the status pill.

items.title: Guidance sounds and taps
items.text:
Two short sounds go with the targets: a click when you reach the yellow camera, and a tone when its area is covered. The "Guidance sounds" switch in Settings, under Guidance, turns them off. The phone's silent switch mutes them as well, and music or podcasts keep playing underneath. The taps you feel on arrival and on completion do not depend on that switch.

"Proximity ticks" are soft taps that come faster as you get nearer to the yellow camera, like a parking sensor, and stop once you are in position. Turn them off in the same section of Settings.

items.title: Minimap
items.text:
What you see. A round map at the bottom left, looking down from above. Your view direction always points up, and a white triangle in the middle is you. The map covers 5 metres around you. Each small square is a patch of known surface, coloured like the dots, with the legend "good" and "needs work" under it. A yellow dot marks the next-view target, with a short arrow towards the area to point at. If the yellow camera is more than 5 metres away, the dot sits on the rim.

What it means. It shows where around you coverage is still weak, including the spots behind you.

What to do. Use it to decide where to walk next, then use the target and the dots for the details. Tap the map to hide it; a round map button takes its place. Tap that to bring the map back.

Screenshot pending: the round minimap at the bottom left with blue and orange squares, the white triangle in the middle, the yellow target dot with its arrow, and the "good" and "needs work" legend.

items.title: Troubleshooting and FAQ
items.text:
Common problems and what to do about them, plus short answers to the questions people ask first.

The camera screen shows problems as dark banners near the top. The symbol tells you the kind: orange arrows when tracking is lost, a yellow tortoise for a hint, a red octagon for an error.

items.title: Tracking is lost
items.text:
What you see. A banner with orange arrows under the status pill. It reads "Relocalising — move back to where you were. Starting a new segment in N s." with a "Start new segment here" button, or "Tracking restarting — a new segment starts when tracking returns." A second banner may read "Move the phone slowly around to start tracking."

Cause. The phone lost track of where it is. Fast movement and scenes with little to see, such as a blank wall, are the usual reasons.

What to do.

  • Walk back to where you were and hold the camera on something with detail. If the phone recognises the place, capture carries on in the same segment.
  • If you do not want to go back, tap "Start new segment here". Capture continues in a new segment with fresh guidance.
  • Do nothing for 15 seconds and the app starts a new segment by itself.

Capturing a scene explains segments in more detail. If the result looks slightly warped, with walls that bend, the camera positions have probably drifted (slid away from the truth) without the app noticing. In general, a shorter capture with plenty of detail in view drifts less.

items.title: Keyframes are not being taken
items.text:
What you see. The frame count in the status pill ("Tracking · 12 frames") stays where it is while you walk.

Cause. Frames are too blurry, or you are standing still. A dim room makes blur worse, because the camera exposes longer.

What to do. Walk and turn more slowly, and add light. If manual capture is on (the hand button on the side rail), the app takes keyframes only when you tap the shutter. Capturing a scene has the details.

items.title: No guidance appears
items.text:
Cause. There are several possible reasons:

  • Nothing to judge yet. The dots, the map and the ring appear a little after you tap Record, and next-view targets wait for 20 seconds after a segment starts.
  • The layer is switched off on the side rail (no white disc behind its button), or the splat view is on. The layers show only while the splat view is off.
  • Hatching also needs LiDAR ("Use LiDAR" on) and a Live splat setting other than "Off".

What to do. Check the buttons on the side rail and wait a little. Reading the guidance describes each layer.

items.title: The guidance is slow and the phone is hot
items.text:
What you see. The dots and targets lag behind what you have just captured, and the phone feels warm.

Cause. With Live splat on "This iPhone", the phone trains the 3D model while it also tracks, films and draws the guidance. In general, an iPhone that gets hot slows itself down to cool off, so the guidance comes later.

What to do.

  • In general, letting the phone cool down in the shade, out of its case, before you go on helps.
  • Turn the dots off with the "Quality dots" button on the side rail; this saves drawing work.
  • For the next capture, set Live splat to "Off" in Settings. The phone then builds no 3D model; the dots, the map, the ring and the next-view targets still work.

If a red banner starting with "Live splat:" appears, the 3D model has a problem. If the banner stays, tap Stop to save your photos; the line above Done may then read "Saved · no splat".

items.title: The camera stopped
items.text:
What you see. A red banner starting with "Camera stopped:" and a "Restart camera" button.

Cause. The camera stopped during the capture.

What to do. Tap "Restart camera".

items.title: "Server and app versions do not match"
items.text:
What you see. This message in a red banner at the top.

Cause. You chose "Mac" under Live splat, and the Mac companion speaks a different version from the app. You see it when the first guidance update from the Mac arrives in a format the app does not know. With "This iPhone" or "Off" you never see it.

What to do. Update both the app and the Mac companion so they match. Until you do, the app cannot read the guidance from the Mac. Capture and export keep working.

items.title: The export is missing or incomplete
items.text:
What you see. One of these:

  • After Stop, the line above Done reads "Save failed · waiting for the splat", "Save failed · no splat", "Splat saved · photos failed" or "Splat on the Mac · photos failed".
  • A red banner reads "Cannot create export folder segment-N: …" or "Export flush failed: …" during the capture.
  • The capture's folder in Files lacks photos you expect.

Cause. The phone could not write the files. In general, the usual cause is a full phone. Closing the app before you tap Stop can also leave the newest photos out of transforms.json.

What to do.

  • Free up space on the phone and capture again.
  • Look in Files under On My iPhone, then "Capture Guide", not iCloud Drive.
  • Always tap Stop before you leave the app. Wait until the button reads "Done" if you want the splat.ply too.
  • If transforms.json misses the newest photos, they are still in images/. Your captures and exporting explains the folder layout.

"Saved · no splat" on its own means the photos are saved but the 3D model could not be written. The capture is still complete for export.

items.title: Which iPhones does it work on?
items.text: Capture Guide was tested on an iPhone 14 Pro. It needs iOS 18 or newer and a phone that supports ARKit, Apple's augmented reality framework. We list no other models.

items.title: Do I need a LiDAR sensor?
items.text: No. The app captures without it. LiDAR adds a depth map to each keyframe and makes the grey hatching possible. On a phone without the sensor, "Use LiDAR" in Settings is greyed out.

items.title: Do I need an internet connection or Wi-Fi?
items.text: No. With Live splat on "This iPhone" or "Off", the capture runs entirely on the phone. Two things use a network. The "Mac" option looks for the Mac companion on your local network, which is why iOS asks for that permission. And to name a capture after its place, the app asks Apple's map service for the place name, which sends the capture's coordinates to Apple. Without a connection the capture is named by date and time, and it gets the place name the next time you open it online. Without location access it keeps the date and time.

items.title: Where is my data stored?
items.text: On the phone, in the Capture Guide folder of the Files app. The app sends your photos nowhere by itself. With Live splat on "Mac", the keyframes go to that Mac over your network. For the place name, the coordinates go to Apple (see above).

items.title: What does Live splat "Off" do?
items.text: The phone builds no 3D model, which keeps it cooler. The capture saves the same photos, and the dots, the map, the ring and the next-view targets still guide you. There is no grey hatching, and the capture's Splat tab says "Live splat was off". You can export and train as usual.

items.title: Is there a Mac app?
items.text: A Mac companion app is planned. Capture Guide does not need it.
